entries.4eb70f7863e73c85a25d76bf1ddd8897e30c9e6d: <div sID="gen17898" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="32" osisID="Jer.32" sID="Jer.32"/> <div eID="gen17898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17899" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17900" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. Jeremiah imprisoned for foretelling the destruction of Jerusalem and the captivity of king Zedekiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.1-Jer.32.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. We have him buying land, by divine appointment, as an assurance that in due time a happy end should be put to the present troubles, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.6-Jer.32.15">ver. 6-15</reference>. III. We have his prayer, which he offered up to God upon that occasion, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.16-Jer.32.25">ver. 16-25</reference>. IV. We have a message which God thereupon entrusted him to deliver to the people. 1. He must foretel the utter destruction of Judah and Jerusalem for their sins, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.26-Jer.32.35">ver. 26-35</reference>. But, 2. At the same time he must assure them that, though the destruction was total, it should not be final, but that at length their posterity should recover the peaceable possession of their own land, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.36-Jer.32.44">ver. 36-44</reference>. The predictions of this chapter, both threatenings and promises, are much the same with what we have already met with again and again, but here are some circumstances that are very particular and remarkable.
entries.c02a625fddc6710b1ed59bbdc1d5a14192026690: <div eID="gen17900" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17899" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Predicted; Jeremiah Imprisoned. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen17901" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word that came to Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar. <hi type="super">2</hi> For then the king of Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem: and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the prison, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the king of Judah's house. <hi type="super">3</hi> For Zedekiah king of Judah had shut him up, saying, Wherefore dost thou prophesy, and say, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall take it; <hi type="super">4</hi> And Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him mouth to mouth, and his eyes shall behold his eyes; <hi type="super">5</hi> And he shall lead Zedekiah to Babylon, and there shall he be until I visit him, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : though ye fight with the Chaldeans, ye shall not prosper. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Jeremiah said, The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">7</hi> Behold, Hanameel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Anathoth: for the right of redemption <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine to buy <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">8</hi> So Hanameel mine uncle's son came to me in the court of the prison according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and said unto me, Buy my field, I pray thee, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Anathoth, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the country of Benjamin: for the right of inheritance <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine, and the redemption <hi type="italic">is</hi> thine; buy <hi type="italic">it</hi> for thyself. Then I knew that this <hi type="italic">was</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> And I bought the field of Hanameel my uncle's son, that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Anathoth, and weighed him the money, <hi type="italic">even</hi> seventeen shekels of silver. <hi type="super">10</hi> And I subscribed the evidence, and sealed <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and took witnesses, and weighed <hi type="italic">him</hi> the money in the balances. <hi type="super">11</hi> So I took the evidence of the purchase, <hi type="italic">both</hi> that which was sealed <hi type="italic">according</hi> to the law and custom, and that which was open: <hi type="super">12</hi> And I gave the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Hanameel mine uncle's <hi type="italic">son,</hi> and in the presence of the witnesses that subscribed the book of the purchase, before all the Jews that sat in the court of the prison. <hi type="super">13</hi> And I charged Baruch before them, saying, <hi type="super">14</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Take these evidences, this evidence of the purchase, both which is sealed, and this evidence which is open; and put them in an earthen vessel, that they may continue many days. <hi type="super">15</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land. <div eID="gen17901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17902" type="x-p"/> It appears by the date of this chapter that we are now coming very nigh to that fatal year which completed the desolations of Judah and Jerusalem by the Chaldeans. God's judgments came gradually upon them, but, they not meeting him by repentance in the way of his judgments, he proceeded in his controversy till all was laid waste, which was in the eleventh year of Zedekiah; now what is here recorded happened in the tenth. The king of Babylon's army had now invested Jerusalem and was carrying on the siege with vigour, not doubting but in a little time to make themselves masters of it, while the besieged had taken up a desperate resolution not to surrender, but to hold out to the last extremity. Now, <div eID="gen17902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17903" type="x-p"/> I. Jeremiah prophesies that both the city and the court shall fall into the hands of the king of Babylon. He tells them expressly that the besiegers shall take the city as a prize, for God, whose city it was in a peculiar manner, will give it into their hands and put it out of his protection (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.3">v. 3</reference>),—that, though Zedekiah attempt to make his escape, he shall be overtaken, and shall be delivered a prisoner into the hands of Nebuchadnezzar, shall be brought into his presence, to his great confusion and terror, he having made himself so obnoxious by breaking his faith with him, he shall hear the king of Babylon pronounce his doom, and see with what fury and indignation he will look upon him (<hi type="italic">His eyes shall behold his eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.4">v. 4</reference>),—that Zedekiah shall be carried to Babylon, and continue a miserable captive there, <hi type="italic">until God visit him,</hi> that is, till God put an end to his life by a natural death, as Nebuchadnezzar had long before put an end to his days by putting out his eyes. Note, Those that live in misery may be truly said to be visited in mercy when God by death takes them home to himself. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> he foretels that all their attempts to force the besiegers from their trenches shall be ineffectual: <hi type="italic">Though you fight with the Chaldeans, you shall not prosper;</hi> how should they, when God did not fight for them? <reference osisRef="Jer.32.5">v. 5</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Jer.34.2-Jer.34.3">ch. xxxiv. 2, 3</reference>. <div eID="gen17903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17904" type="x-p"/> II. For prophesying thus he is imprisoned, not in the common gaol, but in the more creditable prison that was within the verge of the palace, <hi type="italic">in the king of Judah's house,</hi> and there not closely confined, but in <hi type="italic">custodia libera—in the court of the prison,</hi> where he might have good company, good air, and good intelligence brought him, and would be sheltered from the abuses of the mob; but, however, it was a prison, and Zedekiah shut him up in it for prophesying as he did, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.2-Jer.32.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. So far was he from <hi type="italic">humbling himself before Jeremiah,</hi> as he ought to have done (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.12">2 Chron. xxxvi. 12</reference>), that he <hi type="italic">hardened himself</hi> against him. Though he had formerly so far owned him to be a prophet as to desire him to <hi type="italic">enquire of the Lord for them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.21.2">ch. xxi. 2</reference>), yet now he chides him for prophesying (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.3">v. 3</reference>), and shuts him up in prison, perhaps not with design to punish him any further, but only to restrain him from prophesying any further, which was crime enough. Silencing God's prophets, though it is not so bad as mocking and killing them, is yet a great affront to the God of heaven. See how wretchedly the hearts of sinners are hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. Persecution was one of the sins for which God was now contending with them, and yet Zedekiah persists in it even now that he was in the depth of distress. No providences, no afflictions, will of themselves part between men and their sins, unless the grace of God work with them. Nay, some are made worse by those very judgments that should make them better. <div eID="gen17904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17905" type="x-p"/> III. Being in prison, he purchases from a near relation of his a piece of ground that lay in Anathoth, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.6-Jer.32.7">v. 6, 7</reference>, &c. <div eID="gen17905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17906" type="x-p"/> 1. One would not have expected, (1.) That a prophet should concern himself so far in the business of this world; but why not? Though ministers must not entangle themselves, yet they may concern themselves in the affairs of this life. (2.) That one who had neither wife nor children should buy land. We find (<reference osisRef="Jer.16.2">ch. xvi. 2</reference>) that he had no family of his own; yet he may purchase for his own use while he lives, and leave it to the children of his relations when he dies. (3.) One would little have thought that a prisoner should be a purchaser; how should he get money beforehand to buy land with? It is probably that he lived frugally, and saved something out of what belonged to him as a priest, which is no blemish at all to his character; but we have no reason to think that the people were kind, or that his being beforehand was owing to their generosity. Nay, (4.) It was most strange of all that he should buy a <hi type="italic">piece of land</hi> when he himself knew that the whole land was now to be laid waste and fall into the hands of the Chaldeans, and then what good would this do him? But it was the will of God that he should buy it, and he submitted, though the money seemed to be thrown away. His kinsman came to offer it to him; it was not of his own seeking; he coveted not to lay house to house and field to field, but Providence brought it to him, and it was probably a good bargain; besides, the <hi type="italic">right of redemption</hi> belonged to him (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.8">v. 8</reference>), and if he refused he would not do the kinsman's part. It is true he might lawfully refuse, but, being a prophet, in a thing of this nature he must do that which would be for the honour of his profession. <hi type="italic">It became him to fulfil all righteousness.</hi> It was land that lay within the suburbs of a priests' city, and, if he should refuse it, there was danger lest, in these times of disorder, it might be sold to one of another tribe, which was contrary to the law, to prevent which it was convenient for him to buy it. It would likewise be a kindness to his kinsman, who probably was at this time in great want of money. Jeremiah had but a little, but what he had he was willing to lay out in such a manner as might tend most to the honour of God and the good of his friends and country, which he preferred before his own private interests. <div eID="gen17906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17907" type="x-p"/> 2. Two things may be observed concerning this purchase:— <div eID="gen17907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17908" type="x-p"/> (1.) How fairly the bargain was made. When Jeremiah knew by Hanameel's coming to him, as God had foretold he would, that <hi type="italic">it was the word of the Lord,</hi> that it was his mind that he should make this purchase, he made no more difficulty of it, but <hi type="italic">bought the field.</hi> And, [1.] He was very honest and exact in paying the money. He <hi type="italic">weighted him the money,</hi> did not press him to take it upon his report, though he was his near kinsman, but weighed it to him, current money. It was <hi type="italic">seventeen shekels of silver,</hi> amounting to about forty shillings of our money. The land was probably but a little field and of small yearly value, when the purchase was so low; besides, the <hi type="italic">right of inheritance</hi> was in Jeremiah, so that he had only to buy out his kinsman's life, the reversion being his already. Some think this was only the earnest of a greater sum; but we shall not wonder at the smallness of the price if we consider what scarcity there was of money at this time and how little lands were counted upon. [2.] He was very prudent and discreet in preserving the writings. They were subscribed <hi type="italic">before witnesses.</hi> One copy was <hi type="italic">sealed up,</hi> the other was <hi type="italic">open.</hi> One was the original, the other the counterpart; or perhaps that which was <hi type="italic">sealed up</hi> was for his own private use, the other that was <hi type="italic">open</hi> was to be laid up in the public register of conveyances, for any person concerned to consult. Due care and caution in things of this nature might prevent a great deal of injustice and contention. The deeds of purchase were lodged in the hands of Baruch, before witnesses, and he was ordered to lay them up in an <hi type="italic">earthen vessel</hi> (an emblem of the nature of all the securities this world can pretend to give us, brittle things and soon broken), that they might <hi type="italic">continue many days,</hi> for the use of Jeremiah's heirs, after the return out of captivity; for they might then have the benefit of this purchase. Purchasing reversions may be a kindness to those that come after us, and a good man thus <hi type="italic">lays up an inheritance for his children's children.</hi> <div eID="gen17908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17909" type="x-p"/> (2.) What was the design of having this bargain made. It was to signify that though Jerusalem was now besieged, and the whole country was likely to be laid waste, yet the time should come when <hi type="italic">houses, and fields, and vineyards should be again possessed in this land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.15">v. 15</reference>. As God appointed Jeremiah to confirm his predictions of the approaching destruction of Jerusalem by his own practice in living unmarried, so he now appointed him to confirm his predictions of the future restoration of Jerusalem by his own practice in purchasing this field. Note, It concerns ministers to make it to appear in their whole conversation that they do themselves believe that which they preach to others; and that they may do so, and impress it the more deeply upon their hearers, they must many a time deny themselves, as Jeremiah did in both these instances. God having promised that this land should again come into the possession of his people, Jeremiah will, on behalf of his heirs, put in for a share. Note, It is good to manage even our worldly affairs in faith, and to do common business with an eye to the providence and promise of God. Lucius Florus relates it as a great instance of the bravery of the Roman citizens that in the time of the second Punic war, when Hannibal besieged Rome and was very near making himself master of it, a field on which part of his army lay, being offered to sale at that time, was immediately purchased, in a firm belief that the Roman valour would raise the siege, <hi type="italic">lib. ii. cap.</hi> 6. And have not we much more reason to venture our all upon the word of God, and to embark in Zion's interests, which will undoubtedly be the prevailing interests at last? <hi type="italic">Non si male nunc et olim sic erit—Though now we suffer, we shall not suffer always.</hi>
entries.be65be6bebc666e4d6711689b0d2f2f4a094f417: <div eID="gen17909" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeremiah's Prayer. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen17910" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Now when I had delivered the evidence of the purchase unto Baruch the son of Neriah, I prayed unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, <hi type="super">17</hi> Ah Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, <hi type="italic">and</hi> there is nothing too hard for thee: <hi type="super">18</hi> Thou shewest lovingkindness unto thousands, and recompensest the iniquity of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them: the Great, the Mighty God, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, <hi type="italic">is</hi> his name, <hi type="super">19</hi> Great in counsel, and mighty in work: for thine eyes <hi type="italic">are</hi> open upon all the ways of the sons of men: to give every one according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings: <hi type="super">20</hi> Which hast set signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto this day, and in Israel, and among <hi type="italic">other</hi> men; and hast made thee a name, as at this day; <hi type="super">21</hi> And hast brought forth thy people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs, and with wonders, and with a strong hand, and with a stretched out arm, and with great terror; <hi type="super">22</hi> And hast given them this land, which thou didst swear to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey; <hi type="super">23</hi> And they came in, and possessed it; but they obeyed not thy voice, neither walked in thy law; they have done nothing of all that thou commandedst them to do: therefore thou hast caused all this evil to come upon them: <hi type="super">24</hi> Behold the mounts, they are come unto the city to take it; and the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans, that fight against it, because of the sword, and of the famine, and of the pestilence: and what thou hast spoken is come to pass; and, behold, thou seest <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">25</hi> And thou hast said unto me, O Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> , Buy thee the field for money, and take witnesses; for the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen17910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17911" type="x-p"/> We have here Jeremiah's prayer to God upon occasion of the discoveries God had made to him of his purposes concerning this nation, to pull it down, and in process of time to build it up again, which puzzled the prophet himself, who, though he delivered his messages faithfully, yet, in reflecting upon them, was greatly at a loss within himself how to reconcile them; in that perplexity he poured out his soul before God in prayer, and so gave himself ease. That which disturbed him was not the bad bargain he seemed to have made for himself in purchasing a field that he was likely to have no good of, but the case of his people, for whom he was still a kind and faithful intercessor, and he was willing to hope that, if God had so much mercy in store for them hereafter as he had promised, he would not proceed with so much severity against them now as he had threatened. Before Jeremiah went to prayer he delivered the deeds that concerned his new purchase to Baruch, which may intimate to us that when we are going to worship God we should get our minds as clear as may be from the cares and incumbrances of this world. Jeremiah was in prison, in distress, in the dark about the meaning of God's providences, and then he prays. Note, Prayer is a salve for every sore. Whatever is a burden to us, we may by prayer cast it upon the Lord and then be easy. <div eID="gen17911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17912" type="x-p"/> In this prayer, or meditation, <div eID="gen17912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17913" type="x-p"/> I. Jeremiah adores God and his infinite perfections, and gives him the glory due to his name as the Creator, upholder, and benefactor, of the whole creation, thereby owning his irresistible power, that he can do what he will, and his incontestable sovereignty, that he may do what he will, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.17-Jer.32.19">v. 17-19</reference>. Note, When at any time we are perplexed about the particular methods and dispensations of Providence it is good for us to have recourse to our first principles, and to satisfy ourselves with the general doctrines of God's wisdom, power, and goodness. Let us consider, as Jeremiah does here, 1. That God is the fountain of all being, power, life, motion, and perfection: He <hi type="italic">made the heaven and the earth with his outstretched arm;</hi> and therefore who can control him? Who dares contend with him? 2. That with him nothing is impossible, no difficulty insuperable: <hi type="italic">Nothing is too hard for thee.</hi> When human skill and power are quite nonplussed, <hi type="italic">with God are strength and wisdom</hi> sufficient to master all the opposition. 3. That he is a God of boundless bottomless mercy; mercy is his darling attribute; it is his goodness that is his glory: "Thou not only art kind, but thou <hi type="italic">showest lovingkindness,</hi> not to a few, to here and there one, but <hi type="italic">to thousands,</hi> thousands of persons, thousands of generations." 4. That he is a God of impartial and inflexible justice. His reprieves are not pardons, but if in mercy he spares the parents, that they may be led to repentance, yet such a hatred has he to sin, and such a displeasure against sinners, that he <hi type="italic">recompenses their iniquity into the bosom of their children,</hi> and yet does them no wrong; so hateful is the unrighteousness of man, and so jealous of its own honour is the righteousness of God. 5. That he is a God of universal dominion and command: He is <hi type="italic">the great</hi> God, for he is <hi type="italic">the mighty God,</hi> and might among men makes them great. He is <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> of all hosts, that <hi type="italic">is his name,</hi> and he answers to his name, for all the hosts of heaven and earth, of men and angels, are at his beck. 6. That he contrives every thing for the best, and effects every thing as he contrived it: He is <hi type="italic">great in counsel,</hi> so vast are the reaches and so deep are the designs of his wisdom; and he is <hi type="italic">mighty in doing,</hi> according to the counsel of his will. Now such a God as this is not to be quarrelled with. His service is to be constantly adhered to and all his disposals cheerfully acquiesced in. <div eID="gen17913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17914" type="x-p"/> II. He acknowledges the universal cognizance God takes of all the actions of the children of men and the unerring judgment he passes upon them (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy eyes are open upon all the sons of men,</hi> wherever they are, beholding the evil and the good, and upon all <hi type="italic">their ways,</hi> both the course they take and every step they take, not as an unconcerned spectator, but as an observing judge, <hi type="italic">to give every one according to his ways and according</hi> to his deserts, which are <hi type="italic">the fruit of his doings;</hi> for men shall find God as they are found of him. <div eID="gen17914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17915" type="x-p"/> III. He recounts the great things God had done for his people Israel formerly. 1. He brought them out of Egypt, that house of bondage, with <hi type="italic">signs and wonders,</hi> which remain, if not in the marks of them, yet in the memorials of them, <hi type="italic">even unto this day;</hi> for it would never be forgotten, not only <hi type="italic">in Israel,</hi> who were reminded of it every year by the ordinance of the passover, but <hi type="italic">among other men:</hi> all the neighbouring nations spoke of it, as that which redounded exceedingly to the glory of the God of Israel, and made him <hi type="italic">a name as at this day.</hi> This is repeated (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.21">v. 21</reference>), that God <hi type="italic">brought them forth,</hi> not only with comforts and joys to them, but with glory to himself, <hi type="italic">with signs and wonders</hi> (witness the ten plagues), <hi type="italic">with a strong hand,</hi> too strong for the Egyptians themselves, <hi type="italic">and with a stretched-out arm,</hi> that reached Pharaoh, proud as he was, <hi type="italic">and with great terror</hi> to them and all about them. This seems to refer to <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deut. iv. 34</reference>. 2. He brought them into Canaan, that good land, that <hi type="italic">land flowing with milk and honey.</hi> He <hi type="italic">swore to their fathers to give it them,</hi> and, because he would perform his oath, he did give it to the children (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.22">v. 22</reference>) <hi type="italic">and they came in and possessed it.</hi> Jeremiah mentions this both as an aggravation of their sin and disobedience and also as a plea with God to work deliverance for them. Note, It is good for us often to reflect upon the great things that God did for his church formerly, especially in the first erecting of it, that work of wonder. <div eID="gen17915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17916" type="x-p"/> IV. He bewails the rebellions they had been guilty of against God, and the judgments God had brought upon them for these rebellions. It is a sad account he here gives of the ungrateful conduct of that people towards God. He had done every thing that he had promised to do (they had acknowledged it, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.56">1 Kings viii. 56</reference>), but they had <hi type="italic">done nothing of all that he commanded them to do</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.23">v. 23</reference>); they made no conscience of any of <hi type="italic">his laws;</hi> they <hi type="italic">walked not</hi> in them, paid no respect to any of his calls by his prophets, for they <hi type="italic">obeyed not his voice.</hi> And therefore he owns that God was righteous in <hi type="italic">causing all this evil to come upon them.</hi> The city is besieged, is attacked <hi type="italic">by the sword</hi> without, is weakened and wasted by the <hi type="italic">famine</hi> and <hi type="italic">pestilence</hi> within, so that it is ready to fall <hi type="italic">into the hands of the Chaldeans that fight against it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.24">v. 24</reference>); it is <hi type="italic">given into their hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.25">v. 25</reference>. Now, 1. He compares the present state of Jerusalem with the divine predictions, and finds that what God <hi type="italic">has spoken</hi> has <hi type="italic">come to pass.</hi> God had given them fair warning of it before; and, if they had regarded this, the ruin would have been prevented; but, if they will not do what God has commanded, they can expect no other than that he should do what he had threatened. 2. He commits the present state of Jerusalem to the divine consideration and compassion (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold the mounts,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ramparts,</hi> or the <hi type="italic">engines</hi> which they make use of to batter the city and beat down the wall of it. And again, "<hi type="italic">Behold thou seest it,</hi> and takest cognizance of it. Is this the city that thou has chosen to put thy name there? And shall it be thus abandoned?" He neither complains of God for what he had done nor prescribes to God what he should do, but desires he would behold their case, and is pleased to think that he does behold it. Whatever trouble we are in, upon a personal or public account, we may comfort ourselves with this, that God sees it and sees how to remedy it. <div eID="gen17916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17917" type="x-p"/> V. He seems desirous to be let further into the meaning of the order God had now given him to purchase his kinsman's field (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.25">v. 25</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Though the city is given into the hand of the Chaldeans,</hi> and no man is likely to enjoy what he has, yet <hi type="italic">thou hast said unto me, Buy thou the field.</hi>" As soon as he understood that it was the mind of God he did it, and made no objections, was not disobedient to the heavenly vision; but, when he had done it, he desired better to understand why God had ordered him to do it, because the thing looked strange and unaccountable. Note, Though we are bound to follow God with an implicit obedience, yet we should endeavour that it may be more and more an intelligent obedience. We must never dispute God's statutes and judgments, but we may and must enquire, <hi type="italic">What mean these statutes and judgments?</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.6.20">Deut. vi. 20</reference>.
entries.ad822f0d8a4e8a14f05dbe608c2caff6a19c612d: <div eID="gen17917" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Judgments Predicted; Restoration of the Jews; Encouraging Promises. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 589.)</title> <div sID="gen17918" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Then came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Jeremiah, saying, <hi type="super">27</hi> Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of all flesh: is there any thing too hard for me? <hi type="super">28</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans, and into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he shall take it: <hi type="super">29</hi> And the Chaldeans, that fight against this city, shall come and set fire on this city, and burn it with the houses, upon whose roofs they have offered incense unto Baal, and poured out drink offerings unto other gods, to provoke me to anger. <hi type="super">30</hi> For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have only done evil before me from their youth: for the children of Israel have only provoked me to anger with the work of their hands, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">31</hi> For this city hath been to me <hi type="italic">as</hi> a provocation of mine anger and of my fury from the day that they built it even unto this day; that I should remove it from before my face, <hi type="super">32</hi> Because of all the evil of the children of Israel and of the children of Judah, which they have done to provoke me to anger, they, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets, and the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">33</hi> And they have turned unto me the back, and not the face: though I taught them, rising up early and teaching <hi type="italic">them,</hi> yet they have not hearkened to receive instruction. <hi type="super">34</hi> But they set their abominations in the house, which is called by my name, to defile it. <hi type="super">35</hi> And they built the high places of Baal, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to cause their sons and their daughters to pass through <hi type="italic">the fire</hi> unto Molech; which I commanded them not, neither came it into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin. <hi type="super">36</hi> And now therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the God of Israel, concerning this city, whereof ye say, It shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence; <hi type="super">37</hi> Behold, I will gather them out of all countries, whither I have driven them in mine anger, and in my fury, and in great wrath; and I will bring them again unto this place, and I will cause them to dwell safely: <hi type="super">38</hi> And they shall be my people, and I will be their God: <hi type="super">39</hi> And I will give them one heart, and one way, that they may fear me for ever, for the good of them, and of their children after them: <hi type="super">40</hi> And I will make an everlasting covenant with them, that I will not turn away from them, to do them good; but I will put my fear in their hearts, that they shall not depart from me. <hi type="super">41</hi> Yea, I will rejoice over them to do them good, and I will plant them in this land assuredly with my whole heart and with my whole soul. <hi type="super">42</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; Like as I have brought all this great evil upon this people, so will I bring upon them all the good that I have promised them. <hi type="super">43</hi> And fields shall be bought in this land, whereof ye say, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> desolate without man or beast; it is given into the hand of the Chaldeans. <hi type="super">44</hi> Men shall buy fields for money, and subscribe evidences, and seal <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and take witnesses in the land of Benjamin, and in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, and in the cities of the mountains, and in the cities of the valley, and in the cities of the south: for I will cause their captivity to return, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen17918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17919" type="x-p"/> We have here God's answer to Jeremiah's prayer, designed to quiet his mind and make him easy; and it is a full discovery of the purposes of God's wrath against the present generation and the purposes of his grace concerning the future generations. Jeremiah knew not how to <hi type="italic">sing both of mercy and judgment,</hi> but God here teaches to sing unto him of both. When we know not how to reconcile one word of God with another we may yet be sure that both are true, both are pure, both shall be made good, and not one iota or tittle of either shall fall to the ground. When Jeremiah was ordered to buy the field in Anathoth he was willing to hope that God was about to revoke the sentence of his wrath and to order the Chaldeans to raise the siege. "No," says God, "the execution of the sentence shall go on; Jerusalem shall be laid in ruins." Note, Assurances of future mercy must not be interpreted as securities from present troubles. But, lest Jeremiah should think that his being ordered to buy this field intimated that all the mercy God had in store for his people, after their return, was only that they should have the possession of their own land again, he further informs him that that was but a type and figure of those spiritual blessings which should then be abundantly bestowed upon them, unspeakably more valuable than fields and vineyards; so that in this <hi type="italic">word of the Lord,</hi> which came to Jeremiah, we have first as dreadful threatenings and then as precious promises as perhaps any we have in the Old Testament; life and death, good and evil, are here set before us; let us consider and choose wisely. <div eID="gen17919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17920" type="x-p"/> I. The ruin of Judah and Jerusalem is here pronounced. The decree has gone forth, and shall not be recalled. 1. God here asserts his own sovereignty and power (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.27">v. 27</reference>): <hi type="italic">Behold, I am Jehovah,</hi> a self-existent self-sufficient being; <hi type="italic">I am that I am; I am the God of all flesh,</hi> that is, of all mankind, here called <hi type="italic">flesh</hi> because weak and unable to contend with God (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.4">Ps. lvi. 4</reference>), and because wicked and corrupt and unapt to comply with God. God is the Creator of all, and makes what use he pleases of all. He that is the God of Israel is the <hi type="italic">God of all flesh</hi> and of <hi type="italic">the spirits of all flesh,</hi> and, if Israel were cast off, could raise up a people to his name out of some other nation. If he be the <hi type="italic">God of all flesh,</hi> he may well ask, <hi type="italic">Is any thing too hard for me?</hi> What cannot he do from whom all the powers of men are derived, on whom they depend, and by whom all their actions are directed and governed? Whatever he designs to do, whether in wrath or in mercy, nothing can hinder him nor defeat his designs. 2. He abides by that he had often said of the destruction of Jerusalem by the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will give this city into his hand,</hi> now that he is grasping at it, <hi type="italic">and he shall take it</hi> and make a prey of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.29">v. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Chaldeans shall come and set fire to it,</hi> shall burn it and all the <hi type="italic">houses in it,</hi> God's house not excepted, nor the king's neither. 3. He assigns the reason for these severe proceedings against the city that had been so much in his favour. It is sin, it is that and nothing else, that ruins it. (1.) They were impudent and daring in sin. They <hi type="italic">offered incense to Baal,</hi> not in corners, as men ashamed or afraid of being discovered, but upon the <hi type="italic">tops of their houses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.29">v. 29</reference>), in defiance of God's justice. (2.) They designed an affront to God herein. They did it <hi type="italic">to provoke me to anger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.29">v. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">They have only provoked me to anger with the works of their hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.30">v. 30</reference>. They could not promise themselves any pleasure, profit, or honour out of it, but did it on purpose to offend God. And again (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.32">v. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">All the evil which they have done was to provoke me to anger.</hi> They knew he was a jealous God in the matters of his worship, and there they resolved to try his jealousy and dare him to his face. "Jerusalem has been <hi type="italic">to me a provocation of my anger and fury,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.32.31">v. 31</reference>. Their conduct in every thing was provoking. (3.) They began betimes, and had continued all along provoking to God: "They have <hi type="italic">done evil before me from their youth,</hi> ever since they were first formed into a people (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.30">v. 30</reference>), witness their murmurings and rebellions in the wilderness." And as for Jerusalem, though it was the <hi type="italic">holy city,</hi> it has been <hi type="italic">a provocation</hi> to the holy God <hi type="italic">from the day that they built it, even to this day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.31">v. 31</reference>. O what reason have we to lament the little honour God has from this world, and the great dishonour that is done him, when even in Judah, where <hi type="italic">he is known</hi> and <hi type="italic">his name is great,</hi> and in Salem where his <hi type="italic">tabernacle is,</hi> there was always that found that was a provocation to him! (4.) All orders and degrees of men contributed to the common guilt, and therefore were justly involved in the common ruin. Not only the <hi type="italic">children of Israel,</hi> that had revolted from the temple, but the <hi type="italic">children of Judah</hi> too, that still adhered to it—not only the common people, the <hi type="italic">men of Judah</hi> and <hi type="italic">inhabitants of Jerusalem,</hi> but those that should have reproved and restrained sin in others were themselves ringleaders in it, their <hi type="italic">kings</hi> and <hi type="italic">princes,</hi> their <hi type="italic">priests</hi> and <hi type="italic">prophets.</hi> (5.) God had again and again called them to repentance, but they turned a deaf ear to his calls, and rudely turned their back on him that called them, though he was their master, to whom they were bound in duty, and their benefactor, to whom they were bound in gratitude and interest, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.33">v. 33</reference>. "<hi type="italic">I taught them</hi> better manners, with as much care as ever any tender parent taught a child, <hi type="italic">rising up early, in teaching them,</hi> studying to adapt the teaching to their capacities, taking them betimes, when they might have been most pliable, but all in vain; they <hi type="italic">turned not the face to me,</hi> would not so much as look upon me, nay, they <hi type="italic">turned the back upon me,</hi>" an expression of the highest contempt. <hi type="italic">As he called them,</hi> like froward children, <hi type="italic">so they went from him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.2">Hos. xi. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">They have not hearkened to receive instruction;</hi> they regarded not a word that was said to them, though it was designed for their own good. (6.) There was in their idolatries an impious contempt of God; for (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.34">v. 34</reference>) <hi type="italic">they set their abominations</hi> (their idols, which they knew to be in the highest degree abominable to God) <hi type="italic">in the house which is called by my name, to defile it.</hi> They had their idols not only in their high places and groves, but even in God's temple. (7.) They were guilty of the most unnatural cruelty to their own children; for they <hi type="italic">sacrificed them to Moloch,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.35">v. 35</reference>. Thus because they <hi type="italic">liked not to retain God in their knowledge,</hi> but <hi type="italic">changed his glory</hi> into shame, they were justly given up to vile affections and stripped of natural ones, and their glory was turned into shame. And, (8.) What was the consequence of all this? [1.] They <hi type="italic">caused Judah to sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.32.35">v. 35</reference>. The whole country was infected with the contagious idolatries and iniquities of Jerusalem. [2.] They brought ruin upon themselves. It was as if they had done it on purpose that God <hi type="italic">should remove them from before his face</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.31">v. 31</reference>); they would throw themselves out of his favour. <div eID="gen17920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17921" type="x-p"/> II. The restoration of Judah and Jerusalem is here promised, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.36">v. 36</reference>, &c. God will in judgment remember mercy, and there will a time come, a set time, to favour Zion. Observe, 1. The despair to which this people were now at length brought. When the judgment was threatened at a distance they had no fear; when it attacked them they had no hope. They said concerning the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.36">v. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">It shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon,</hi> not by any cowardice or ill conduct of ours, but by <hi type="italic">the sword, famine, and pestilence.</hi> Concerning the country they said, with vexation (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.43">v. 43</reference>), <hi type="italic">It is desolate, without man or beast;</hi> there is no relief, there is no remedy. <hi type="italic">It is given into the hand of the Chaldeans.</hi> Note, Deep security commonly ends in deep despair; whereas those that keep up a holy fear at all times have a good hope to support them in the worst of times. 2. The hope that God gives them of mercy which he had in store for them hereafter. Though their carcases must fall in captivity, yet their children after them shall again see this good land and the goodness of God in it. (1.) They shall be brought up from their captivity and shall come and settle again in this land, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.37">v. 37</reference>. They had been under God's <hi type="italic">anger and fury, and great wrath;</hi> but now they shall partake of his grace, and love, and great favour. He had dispersed them, and <hi type="italic">driven them into all countries.</hi> Those that fled dispersed themselves; those that fell into the enemies; hands were dispersed by them, in policy, to prevent combinations among them. God's hand was in both. But now God will find them out, and <hi type="italic">gather them out of all the countries whither they were driven,</hi> as he promised in the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.3-Deut.30.4">Deut. xxx. 3, 4</reference>) and the saints had prayed, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Ps. cvi. 47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.1.9">Neh. i. 9</reference>. He had banished them, but he will <hi type="italic">bring them again to this place,</hi> which they could not but have an affection for. For many years past, while they were in their own land, they were continually exposed, and terrified with the alarms of war; but now <hi type="italic">I will cause them to dwell safely.</hi> Being reformed, and having returned to God, neither their own consciences within nor their enemies without shall be a terror to them. He promises (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.41">v. 41</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will plant them in this land assuredly;</hi> not only I will certainly do it, but they shall here enjoy a holy a security and repose, and they shall take root here, shall be <hi type="italic">planted in stability,</hi> and not again be unfixed and shaken. (2.) God will renew his covenant with them, a covenant of grace, the blessings of which are spiritual, and such as will work good things in them, to qualify them for the great things God intended to do for them. It is called an <hi type="italic">everlasting covenant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.40">v. 40</reference>), not only because God will be for ever faithful to it, but because the consequences of it will be everlasting. For, doubtless, here the promises look further than to Israel according to the flesh, and are sure to all believers, to every Israelite indeed. Good Christians may apply them to themselves and plead them with God, may claim the benefit of them and take the comfort of them. [1.] God will own them for his, and make over himself to them to be theirs (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.38">v. 38</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall be my people.</hi> He will make them his by working in them all the characters and dispositions of his people, and then he will protect, and guide, and govern them as his people. "And, to make them truly, completely, and eternally happy, <hi type="italic">I will be their God.</hi>" They shall serve and worship God as theirs and cleave to him only, and he will approve himself theirs. All he is, all he has, shall be engaged and employed for their good. [2.] God will give them a heart to fear him, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.39">v. 39</reference>. That which he requires of those whom he takes into covenant with him as his people is that they fear him, that they reverence his majesty, dread his wrath, stand in awe of his authority, pay homage to him, and give him the glory due unto his name. Now what God requires of them he here promises to work in them, pursuant to his choice of them as his people. Note, As it is God's prerogative to fashion men's hearts, so it is his promise to his people to fashion theirs aright; and a heart to fear God is indeed a good heart, and well fashioned. It is repeated (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.40">v. 40</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will put my fear in their hearts,</hi> that is, work in them gracious principles and dispositions, that shall influence and govern their whole conversation. Teachers may put good things into our heads, but it is God only that can put them into our hearts, that can work in us <hi type="italic">both to will and to do.</hi> [3.] He will <hi type="italic">give them one heart and one way.</hi> In order to their walking in one way, he will give them one heart: as the heart is, so will the way be, and both shall be one; that is <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They shall be each of them one with themselves. <hi type="italic">One heart</hi> is the same with a <hi type="italic">new heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.11.19">Ezek. xi. 19</reference>. The heart is <hi type="italic">then</hi> one when it is fully determined for God and entirely devoted to God. When the eye is single and God's glory alone aimed at, when our hearts are fixed, trusting in God, and we are uniform and universal in our obedience to him, then the heart is one and way one; and, unless the heart be thus steady, the goings will not be stedfast. From this promise we may take direction and encouragement to pray, with David (<reference osisRef="Ps.86.11">Ps. lxxxvi. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Unite my heart to fear thy name;</hi> for God says, <hi type="italic">I will give them one heart, that they may fear me. Secondly,</hi> They shall be all of them one with each other. All good Christians shall be incorporated into one body; Jews and Gentiles shall become <hi type="italic">one sheep-fold;</hi> and they shall all, as far as they are sanctified, have a disposition to love one another, the gospel they profess having in it the strongest inducements to mutual love, and the Spirit that dwells in them being the Spirit of love. Though they may have different apprehensions about minor things, they shall be all one in the great things of God, being renewed after the same image. Though they may have many paths, they have but <hi type="italic">one way,</hi> that of serious godliness. [4.] He will effectually provide for their perseverance in grace and the perpetuating of the covenant between himself and them. They would have been happy when there were first planted in Canaan, like Adam in paradise, if they had not departed from God. And therefore, now that they are restored to their happiness, they shall be confirmed in it by the preventing of their departures from God, and this will complete their bliss. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God will never leave nor forsake them: <hi type="italic">I will not turn away from them to do them good.</hi> Earthly princes are fickle, and their greatest favourites have fallen under their frowns; but God's <hi type="italic">mercy endures for ever. Whom he loves he loves to the end.</hi> God may seem to turn from this people (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.8">Isa. liv. 8</reference>), but even then he does not turn from doing and designing them good. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They shall never leave nor forsake him; that is the thing we are in danger of. We have no reason to distrust God's fidelity and constancy, but our own; and therefore it is here promised that God will <hi type="italic">give them a heart to fear him for ever,</hi> all days, to be in his fear every day and all the day long (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.17">Prov. xxiii. 17</reference>), and to continue so to the end of their days. He will put such a principle into their hearts that they <hi type="italic">shall not depart from him.</hi> Even those who have given up their names to God, if they be left to themselves, will depart from him; but the fear of God ruling in the heart, will prevent their departure. That, and nothing else, will do it. If we continue close and faithful to God, it is owing purely to his almighty grace and not to any strength or resolution of our own. [5.] He will entail a blessing upon their seed, will give them grace to fear him, <hi type="italic">for the good of them and of their children after them.</hi> As their departures from God had been to the prejudice of their children, so their adherence to God should be to the advantage of their children. We cannot better consult the good of posterity than by setting up, and keeping up, the fear and worship of God in our families. [6.] He will take a pleasure in their prosperity and will do every thing to advance it (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.41">v. 41</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will rejoice over them to do them good.</hi> God will certainly do them good because he rejoices over them. They are dear to him; he makes his boast of them, and therefore will not only do them good, but will delight in doing them good. When he punishes them it is with reluctance. <hi type="italic">How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?</hi> But, when he restores them, it is with satisfaction; he rejoices in doing them good. We ought therefore to serve him with pleasure and to rejoice in all opportunities of serving him. He is himself a cheerful giver, and therefore loves a cheerful servant. <hi type="italic">I will plant them</hi> (says God) <hi type="italic">with my whole heart and with my whole soul.</hi> He will be intent upon it, and take delight in it; he will make it the business of his providence to settle them again in Canaan, and the various dispensations of providence shall concur to it. All things shall appear at last so to have been working for the good of the church that it will be said, The governor of the world is entirely taken up with the care of his church. [7.] These promises shall as surely be performed as the foregoing threatenings were; and the accomplishment of those, notwithstanding the security of the people, might confirm their expectation of the performance of these, notwithstanding their present despair (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.42">v. 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">As I have brought all this great evil upon them,</hi> pursuant to the threatenings, and for the glory of divine justice, <hi type="italic">so I will bring upon them all this good,</hi> pursuant to the promise, and for the glory of divine mercy. He that is faithful to his threatenings will much more be so to his promises; and he will comfort his people <hi type="italic">according to the time that he has afflicted them.</hi> The churches shall have rest after the days of adversity. [8.] As an earnest of all this, houses and lands shall again fetch a good price in Judah and Jerusalem, and, though now they are a drug, there shall again be a sufficient number of purchasers (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.43-Jer.32.44">v. 43, 44</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fields shall be bought in this land,</hi> and people will covet to have lands here rather than any where else. Lands, wherever they lie, will go off, not only in <hi type="italic">the places about Jerusalem,</hi> but <hi type="italic">in the cities of Judah</hi> and of Israel, too, whether they lie <hi type="italic">on mountains,</hi> or in valleys, or <hi type="italic">in the south,</hi> in all parts of the country, <hi type="italic">men shall buy fields, and subscribe evidences.</hi> Trade shall revive, for they shall have money enough to buy land with. Husbandry shall revive, for those that have money shall covet to lay it out upon lands. Laws shall again have their due course, for they shall <hi type="italic">subscribe evidences and seal them.</hi> This is mentioned to reconcile Jeremiah to his new purchase. Though he had bought a piece of ground and could not go to see it, yet he must believe that this was the pledge of many a purchase, and those but faint resemblances of the purchased possessions in the heavenly Canaan, reserved for all those who have God's fear in their hearts and do not depart from him.  <chapter eID="Jer.32"/> <div eID="gen17921" type="x-p"/>

entries.649837bc4477164ffc92308dda47d60abb5efd84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10291"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 32</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.32.1-Jer.32.14">Jr 32:1-14</reference>. Jeremiah, Imprisoned for His Prophecy against Jerusalem, Buys a Patrimonial Property (His Relative Hanameel's), IN Order to Certify to the Jews Their Future Return from Babylon.</title> <div sID="gen18371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10291"/><hi type="bold">1. tenth year--</hi>The siege of Jerusalem had already begun, in the tenth month of the ninth year of Zedekiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.1">Jr 39:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.1">2Ki 25:1</reference>). <div eID="gen18371" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebb6edab55d48a9af239ffe348af1ecbf8ebc4d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10292"/><div sID="gen18372" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10292"/><hi type="bold">2. in ... court of ... prison--</hi>that is, in the open space occupied by the guard, from which he was not allowed to depart, but where any of his friends might visit him (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.12">Jr 32:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.38.13">Jr 38:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.28">28</reference>). Marvellous obstinacy, that at the time when they were experiencing the truth of Jeremiah's words in the pressure of the siege, they should still keep the prophet in confinement [Calvin]. The circumstances narrated (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.3-Jer.32.5">Jr 32:3-5</reference>) occurred at the beginning of the siege, when Jeremiah foretold the capture of the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.1">Jr 32:1</reference>; Jr 34:1-7; 39:1). He was at that time put into free custody in the court of the prison. At the raising of the siege by Pharaoh-hophra, Jeremiah was on the point of repairing to Benjamin, when he was cast into "the dungeon," but obtained leave to be removed again to the court of the prison (<reference osisRef="Jer.37.12-Jer.37.21">Jr 37:12-21</reference>). When there he urged the Jews, on the second advance of the Chaldeans to the siege, to save themselves by submission to Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.2">Jr 38:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.38.3">3</reference>); in consequence of this the king, at the instigation of the princes, had him cast into a miry dungeon (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.4-Jer.38.6">Jr 38:4-6</reference>); again he was removed to the prison court at the intercession of a courtier (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.7-Jer.32.13">Jr 32:7-13</reference>), where he remained till the capture of the city (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.28">Jr 32:28</reference>), when he was liberated (<reference osisRef="Jer.39.11">Jr 39:11</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Jer.40.1">Jr 40:1</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen18372" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a2fa50ba03e94287eff0799a53232d552c54838: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10293"/><div sID="gen18373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10293"/><hi type="bold">4. his eyes shall behold his eyes--</hi>that is, only before reaching Babylon, which he was not to see. <reference osisRef="Jer.39.6">Jr 39:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.39.7">7</reference> harmonizes this prophecy (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.4">Jr 32:4</reference>) with the seemingly opposite prophecy, <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.13">Eze 12:13</reference>, "He shall not see." <div eID="gen18373" type="x-p"/>
entries.9443df0b753cadd56f9d072adb5dccef96860ea9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10294"/><div sID="gen18374" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10294"/><hi type="bold">5. visit him--</hi>in a good sense (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.22">Jr 27:22</reference>); referring to the honor paid Zedekiah at his death and burial (<reference osisRef="Jer.34.4">Jr 34:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.5">5</reference>). Perhaps, too, before his death he was treated by Nebuchadnezzar with some favor.<div eID="gen18374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">though ye fight ... shall not prosper--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.21.4">Jr 21:4</reference>). <div eID="gen18375" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f174dddd2e0c14178fb5e3d6659f5faeeb191a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10295"/><div sID="gen18376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10295"/><hi type="bold">6. Jeremiah said--</hi>resuming the thread of <reference osisRef="Jer.32.1">Jr 32:1</reference>, which was interrupted by the parenthesis (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.2-Jer.32.5">Jr 32:2-5</reference>). <div eID="gen18376" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a1b11f491b3b905605dc6d7490cc0e68896fcf4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10296"/><div sID="gen18377" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10296"/><hi type="bold">7. son of Shallum thine uncle--</hi>therefore, Jeremiah's first cousin.<div eID="gen18377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18378" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">field ... in Anathoth--</hi>a sacerdotal city: and so having one thousand cubits of suburban fields outside the wall attached to it (<reference osisRef="Num.35.4">Nu 35:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.35.5">5</reference>). The prohibition to sell these suburban fields (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.34">Le 25:34</reference>) applied merely to their alienating them from Levites to another tribe; so that this chapter does not contravene that prohibition. Besides, what is here meant is only the purchase of the use of the field till the year of jubilee. On the failure of the owner, the next of kin had the right of redeeming it (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.25">Le 25:25</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Ruth.4.3-Ruth.4.6">Ru 4:3-6</reference>). <div eID="gen18378" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e6d461f275d55eee7bc7dcb5fabb5b41d443b32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10297"/><div sID="gen18379" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10297"/><hi type="bold">8. Then I knew--</hi>Not that Jeremiah previously doubted the reality of the divine communication, but, the effect following it, and the prophet's experimentally knowing it, confirmed his faith and was the seal to the vision. The Roman historian, Florus (2.6), records a similar instance: During the days that Rome was being besieged by Hannibal, the very ground on which he was encamped was put up for sale at Rome, and found a purchaser; implying the calm confidence of the ultimate issue entertained by the Roman people. <div eID="gen18379" type="x-p"/>
entries.5cad4abf52a7988da220968dc1293e9e8d81caa7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10298"/><div sID="gen18380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10298"/><hi type="bold">9. seventeen shekels of silver--</hi>As the shekel was only 2s. 4d.., the whole would be under £2, a rather small sum, even taking into account the fact of the Chaldean occupation of the land, and the uncertainty of the time when it might come to Jeremiah or his heirs. Perhaps the "seven shekels," which in the Hebrew (see Margin) are distinguished from the "ten pieces of silver," were shekels of gold [Maurer]. <div eID="gen18380" type="x-p"/>
entries.f3e3e9c2e202edc19a4346a5c4e1f491f7be92f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10299"/><div sID="gen18381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10299"/><hi type="bold">10. subscribed--</hi>I wrote in the deed, "book of purchase" (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.12">Jr 32:12</reference>).<div eID="gen18381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">weighed--</hi>coined money was not in early use; hence money was "weighed" (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.16">Ge 23:16</reference>). <div eID="gen18382" type="x-p"/>
entries.842036143f00118027deade795e136e132e1b027: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10300"/><div sID="gen18383" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10300"/><hi type="bold">11. evidence ... sealed ... open--</hi>Two deeds were drawn up in a contract of sale; the one, the original copy, witnessed and sealed with the public seal; the other not so, but open, and therefore less authoritative, being but a copy. Gataker thinks that the purchaser sealed the one with his own seal; the other he showed to witnesses that they might write their names on the back of it and know the contents; and that some details, for example, the conditions and time of redemption were in the sealed copy, which the parties might not choose to be known to the witnesses, and which were therefore not in the open copy. The sealed copy, when opened after the seventy years' captivity, would greatly confirm the faith of those living at that time. The "law and custom" refer, probably, not merely to the sealing up of the conditions and details of purchase, but also to the law of redemption, according to which, at the return to Judea, the deed would show that Jeremiah had bought the field by his right as next of kin (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.13-Lev.25.16">Le 25:13-16</reference>), [Ludovicus De Dieu]. <div eID="gen18383" type="x-p"/>
entries.70995fd667f8b3476ff2d71f48bdd270334b1d98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10301"/><div sID="gen18384" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10301"/><hi type="bold">12. Baruch--</hi>Jeremiah's amanuensis and agent (<reference osisRef="Jer.36.4">Jr 36:4</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen18384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18385" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before all--</hi>In sales everything clandestine was avoided; publicity was required. So here, in the court of prison, where Jeremiah was confined, there were soldiers and others, who had free access to him, present (<reference osisRef="Jer.38.1">Jr 38:1</reference>). <div eID="gen18385" type="x-p"/>
entries.3821ed29f703c5b66d498c1e6ad1e00a0fe6056f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10302"/><div sID="gen18386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10302"/><hi type="bold">14. in an earthen vessel--</hi>that the documents might not be injured by the moisture of the surrounding earth; at the same time, being buried, they could not be stolen, but would remain as a pledge of the Jews' deliverance until God's time should come. <div eID="gen18386" type="x-p"/>
entries.7810c92e4c0a709a28dc45d6e659268a48a46e72: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10303"/><div sID="gen18387" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10303"/>15. (Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.32.24">Jr 32:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.37">25, 37</reference>, 43, 44). <div eID="gen18387" type="x-p"/>
entries.177e10819da80a0d364b7544988a633477600936: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10304"/><div sID="gen18388" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10304"/>16. Jeremiah, not comprehending how God's threat of destroying Judah could be reconciled with God's commanding him to purchase land in it as if in a free country, has recourse to his grand remedy against perplexities, prayer. <div eID="gen18388" type="x-p"/>
entries.9a1863dab3c6deb26720c941188479fab571e386: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10305"/><div sID="gen18389" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10305"/><hi type="bold">17. hast made ... heaven--</hi>Jeremiah extols God's creative power, as a ground of humility on his part as man: It is not my part to call Thee, the mighty God, to account for Thy ways (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jr 12:1</reference>).<div eID="gen18389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18390" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">too hard--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Jer.32.27">Jr 32:27</reference> God's reply exactly accords with Jeremiah's prayer (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.14">Ge 18:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.6">Zec 8:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.37">Lu 1:37</reference>). <div eID="gen18390" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef51101fdce6e5593b97f4a68315d803c6f87e42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10306"/><div sID="gen18391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10306"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.7">Ex 34:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.6">Is 65:6</reference>). This is taken from the decalogue (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.6">6</reference>). This is a second consideration to check hasty judgments as to God's ways: Thou art the gracious and righteous Judge of the world. <div eID="gen18391" type="x-p"/>
entries.e0c5930123c5936b4a2524c1bddda6dd0fbcfd45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10307"/><div sID="gen18392" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10307"/><hi type="bold">19. counsel ... work--</hi>devising ... executing (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.29">Is 28:29</reference>).<div eID="gen18392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18393" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes ... open upon all--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.34.21">Job 34:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.21">Pr 5:21</reference>).<div eID="gen18393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18394" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to give ... according to ... ways--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jr 17:10</reference>). <div eID="gen18394" type="x-p"/>
entries.1355f89ec0f8cbdd82f67140e569fc5477ec88eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10308"/><div sID="gen18395" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10308"/><hi type="bold">20. even unto this day--</hi>Thou hast given "signs" of Thy power from the day when Thou didst deliver Israel out of Egypt by mighty miracles, down to the present time [Maurer]. Calvin explains it, "memorable even unto this day."<div eID="gen18395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18396" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among other men--</hi>not in Israel only, but among foreign peoples also. Compare for "other" understood, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.5">Psa 73:5</reference>.<div eID="gen18396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18397" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made thee a name--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.9.16">Ex 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.21">1Ch 17:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.12">Is 63:12</reference>).<div eID="gen18397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18398" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as at this day--</hi>a name of power, such as Thou hast at this day. <div eID="gen18398" type="x-p"/>
entries.51f3a09fa3a15a31ecbe52982002bd8ab3436d88: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10309"/><div sID="gen18399" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10309"/>21. (<reference osisRef="Ps.136.11">Psa 136:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.136.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen18399" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7baf33f9e0628a013cb06bbeacded77c3970f99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10310"/><div sID="gen18400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10310"/><hi type="bold">22. given ... didst swear--</hi>God gave it by a gratuitous covenant, not for their deserts.<div eID="gen18400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18401" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a land flowing with milk and honey--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Num.14.8">Nu 14:8</reference>). <div eID="gen18401" type="x-p"/>
entries.9176558a37d1eec609439033196eef2a13eb3659: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10311"/><div sID="gen18402" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10311"/><hi type="bold">23. all ... thou commandedst ... all this evil--</hi>Their punishment was thus exactly commensurate with their sin. It was not fortuitous. <div eID="gen18402" type="x-p"/>
entries.143f36b25a6fb11ebf44e4ded3d1f17cd4c0e7fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10312"/><div sID="gen18403" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10312"/><hi type="bold">24. mounts--</hi>mounds of earth raised as breastworks by the besieging army, behind which they employed their engines, and which they gradually pushed forward to the walls of the city.<div eID="gen18403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18404" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold, thou seest it--</hi>connected with <reference osisRef="Jer.32.25">Jr 32:25</reference>. Thou seest all this with Thine own eyes, and yet (what seems inconsistent with it) Thou commandest me to buy a field. <div eID="gen18404" type="x-p"/>
entries.9568483ce0e02fee474bf9ef658a1078941d0fbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10313"/><div sID="gen18405" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10313"/><hi type="bold">25. for the city, &c.--</hi>rather, "though," &c. <div eID="gen18405" type="x-p"/>
entries.4281c0e6266eaf1bb8565c63248aa6921a91a023: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10314"/><div sID="gen18406" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10314"/>27. Jehovah retorts Jeremiah's own words: I am indeed, as thou sayest (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.17">Jr 32:17</reference>), the God and Creator of "all flesh," and "nothing is too hard for Me"; thine own words ought to have taught thee that, though Judea and Jerusalem are given up to the Chaldeans now for the sins of the Jews, yet it will not be hard to Me, when I please, to restore the state so that houses and lands therein shall be possessed in safety (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.36-Jer.32.44">Jr 32:36-44</reference>). <div eID="gen18406" type="x-p"/>
entries.1427df83a541beaf714dbdda5606ce81489e09aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10315"/><div sID="gen18407" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10315"/><hi type="bold">29. burn ... houses upon whose roofs ... incense unto Baal--</hi>retribution in kind. They burnt incense to Baal, on the houses, so the houses shall be burnt (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.13">Jr 19:13</reference>). The god of fire was the object of their worship; so fire shall be the instrument of their punishment.<div eID="gen18407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18408" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to provoke me--</hi>indicating the design, not merely the event. They seemed to court God's "anger," and purposely to "provoke" Him. <div eID="gen18408" type="x-p"/>
entries.60df37b1e5165c4c6dfae676d570ca7ffd93fd20: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10316"/><div sID="gen18409" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10316"/><hi type="bold">30. have ... done--</hi>literally, "have been doing"; implying continuous action.<div eID="gen18409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18410" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">only ... evil ... only provoked me--</hi>They have been doing nothing else but evil; their sole aim seems to have been to provoke Me.<div eID="gen18410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18411" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their youth--</hi>the time when they were in the wilderness, having just before come into national existence. <div eID="gen18411" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4ce2c7e055faa39716cb6e5e5f72778d2ac9c0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10317"/><div sID="gen18412" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10317"/><hi type="bold">31. provocation of mine anger--</hi>literally, "for mine anger." Calvin, therefore, connects these words with those at the end of the verse, "this city has been to me an object for mine anger (namely, by reason of the provocations mentioned, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.30">Jr 32:30</reference>, &c.), that I should remove it," &c. Thus, there will not be the repetition of the sentiment, <reference osisRef="Jer.32.30">Jr 32:30</reference>, as in English Version; the Hebrew also favors this rendering. However, Jeremiah delights in repetitions. In English Version the words, "that I should remove it," &c., stand independently, as the result of what precedes. The time is ripe for taking vengeance on them (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.27">2Ki 23:27</reference>).<div eID="gen18412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18413" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the day that they built it--</hi>Solomon completed the building of the city; and it was he who, first of the Jewish kings, turned to idolatry. It was originally built by the idolatrous Canaanites. <div eID="gen18413" type="x-p"/>
entries.e49cda2f4c99c44dd9bbe23d816ff5e1592f3cd9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10318"/><div sID="gen18414" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10318"/><hi type="bold">32. priests ... prophets--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Neh.9.32">Ne 9:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.9.34">34</reference>). Hence, learn, though ministers of God apostatize, we must remain faithful. <div eID="gen18414" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fa8fdd7c73a861b024a511095e1b36ce5ee8c41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10319"/><div sID="gen18415" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10319"/>33. (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jr 2:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.13">7:13</reference>). <div eID="gen18415" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f94f68db07b3055c197241d97a1431e03434ea3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10320"/><div sID="gen18416" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10320"/>34. (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.30">Jr 7:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.5-Ezek.8.17">Eze 8:5-17</reference>). <div eID="gen18416" type="x-p"/>
entries.03c6f67902f7dc3fb4ad0109acc4276be6900dae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10321"/><div sID="gen18417" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10321"/><hi type="bold">35. cause ... pass through ... fire--</hi>By way of purification, they passed through with bare feet (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Le 18:21</reference>).<div eID="gen18417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18418" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Molech--</hi>meaning "king"; the same as Milcom (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.33">1Ki 11:33</reference>).<div eID="gen18418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I commanded ... not--</hi>This cuts off from the superstitious the plea of a good intention. All "will-worship" exposes to God's wrath (<reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col 2:18</reference>, 23). <div eID="gen18419" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2d88fb82336cdbfb0aa63c746f17281e1d32d28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10322"/><div sID="gen18420" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10322"/><hi type="bold">36. And now therefore--</hi>rather, "But now, nevertheless." Notwithstanding that their guilt deserves lasting vengeance, God, for the elect's sake and for His covenant's sake, will, contrary to all that might have been expected, restore them.<div eID="gen18420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18421" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye say, It shall be delivered into ... king of Babylon--</hi>The reprobate pass from the extreme of self-confidence to that of despair of God's fulfilling His promise of restoring them. <div eID="gen18421" type="x-p"/>
entries.670452f25ce514bc4d35f37de824510b14c56e7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10323"/><div sID="gen18422" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10323"/>37. (See on <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">Jr 16:15</reference>). The "all" countries implies a future restoration of Israel more universal than that from Babylon. <div eID="gen18422" type="x-p"/>
